newsitem.title: BRAZIL: We are whales, not tigers, says Brazil's Cardoso.
newsitem.headline: We are whales, not tigers, says Brazil's Cardoso.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso dismissed comparisons between Latin America's largest economy and Asian countries suffering currency woes, O Globo newspaper reported on Wednesday.

Globo columnist Miriam Leitao also wrote that Cardoso threw his full weight behind the government's foreign exchange and monetary policies, chastising outspoken Communications Minister Sergio Motta in the process.

"We are not tigers. We are a whale which moves slowly, but with firmness, we do not leap like cats," the president said in an interview with Leitao, referring to the so-called "Asian Tigers" who have fallen prey to currency speculators.

Motta's ministry denied in a hastily-issued statement Tuesday evening that he had criticized Central Bank Director of International Affairs Gustavo Franco for putting economic stability above economic development.
Several reporters said they had the minister recorded on tape.
Motta's reported comments were widely blamed for accentuating an already-sharp plunge in Brazilian stocks Tuesday because they implied a split in the government over policy.

Cardoso rebuffed his ebullient minister, a close friend of the president known familiarly as the "Tractor" because of his tendency to put his foot in his mouth and to ruffle feathers at sensitive moments.
"The foreign exchange policy is mine, has my support and nothing here is done without my approval," Cardoso said in the Globo interview.
"Everyone who has a position of command in the economic team -- and at the end of the day I'm the one who gives the orders -- agrees that this is the right policy."

Newspapers reported that Finance Minister Pedro Malan, in Washington for talks with International Monetary Fund officials, and Gustavo Franco, trying in vain to enjoy a holiday in Rio de Janeiro, were furious at Motta's faux pas.
Brazilian markets bounced back Wednesday on rumors of heavy buying by the National Development Bank (BNDES).
Profit-taking stemming from recent devaluations by Thailand and the Philippines and currency jitters in other emerging markets shaved some 12 percent off the Sao Paulo bolsa on Monday and Tuesday.
Central Bank officials denied they planned any steep devaluation of the real and stuck to their view that the drop in share prices was a natural correction to an overbought market.
